Everything else has already become mere façade—above all, the image of Leviathan.
To live off another person’s guilt is the lowest possible way of living at another person’s expense.

To live from fines, penalties, and blood-money is the dirtiest possible way of taking booty. But this is how they have always lived: from the confiscated property of proscribed enemies and enemies placed hors la loi, outside the law.
The particular idea of booty that belongs to civil war.

The victor’s claim to compensation. There is no triumph in civil war. It was already considered offensive that, during Caesar’s triumph in September of the year 46, Cato’s suicide was displayed in an image (Ed. Meyer, p. 38), even though the triumph was presented not as a triumph over defeated Roman citizens but as a fourfold victory over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus, and Numidia.
On James Burnham’s The Managerial Revolution: These are discoveries we made twenty or thirty years ago.
If freedom depends on the existence of opposition, who organizes the opposition when everything is organized and even what remains unorganized becomes nothing more than a protected nature reserve?

Does the opposition organize itself freely? Then the ruling elite no longer has it under control. Or is the ruler himself supposed to organize his own opposition, as under Kemal Pasha? Then the whole thing is rigged.

The decisive fact remains that the pressure toward conscious organization, bureaucracy, and planning becomes total. That is Burnham’s starting point too. That is what is current, realistic, suited to the age, and free of illusions.

Why, then, does he suddenly turn toward this contradictory optimism about opposition? How tiny, how minimal, the room left for opposition becomes under total planning! This is still the old idea of opposition that belongs to the spatial imagination of a maritime empire whose ruling class can divide the wealth of the earth among itself—with a free ocean still available!
Once things become serious and bare survival is at stake, games like that come to an end.

The most astonishing example of historical dialectic is one that today’s Hegelians have failed to see even though it stands directly before their eyes: within an empire based on sailing ships—essentially an empire without machines—the machine and the Industrial Revolution arise.
The philosophy of the “I” is an enormous lever for prying the world off its hinges.
If I am transcendental consciousness—and surely I must be, since otherwise I could not even deny that I am—then why should I not myself be the Ens Perfectissimum, the most perfect being?
Why should I not apply to Myself all the arguments of the ontological proof of God?
The ontological proof of God would then prove that I am God.
The splendour of this earthly world is easy enough to argue for.
The only thing I inherit is my own body.
The only thing I possess is this one, unnameable instant, lost the moment it arrives.

“In the end I must withdraw even the half-adequate language I have been using, language I intended to use only for as long as I was still digging around in the entrails of law and at least allowing the word itself to remain.
But once the concept disappears, the word itself truly loses its meaning.
A right can be granted only by a spirit—by God, humanity, or divinity. I demand no right, and therefore I need recognize none.
With absolute right, right itself disappears. The rule of the very concept of right is abolished. I am simply powerful.
If I am powerful, then I am already authorized by that fact alone.
Right is a fixed idea granted by a ghost.
Right is an act of grace bestowed by the judge.
Power and force exist only in Me, the powerful and forceful one.”
That—and nothing else—is the splendour of this earthly world.
As long as a man enjoys honour among other people, as the famous Rilke did, he will find this earthly life splendid despite every bodily suffering.
But wait and see how the world looks to him once he has been dishonoured and stripped of his rights.
The moment we succeed in reaching the contemplative position, we are forced to find the world not merely bearable but magnificent. There it is: the Ens perfectissimum.
The best of all possible worlds.
Beautiful to look at and terrible to be.
But anyone who does not want merely to contemplate the world but to change it must necessarily find the world in need of change—which means bad.
I am disgusted by the pathos of moral outrage that arises when someone wants to create the world anew so that he can indulge his will to power and destroy his enemies.

Werner Kaegi, “Problems of the Rule-of-Law State” (Universitas, August 1947), argues that the abolition of the right of resistance—the great showpiece achievement of the modern state—has now been reversed beneath the shadow of Leviathan, and that the problem of resistance has perhaps never been more urgent.
“As the level of the rule-of-law state falls, the level of the right of resistance rises; when resistance within the constitution fails, resistance outside the constitution appears.”
But, I believe, His Lordship wrote this more bravely than he would have acted on it.
Compare Hobbes’s reply to Bishop Bramhall (pp. 436, 454, 1750 edition).
Where was His Lordship when he wrote this?
Germany in 1938? Or Switzerland in 1948? So once again: the problem of legality and legitimacy.
Has he understood the problem of legality at all “in the shadow of Leviathan”?
Has he himself ever been in a situation of resistance?
Resistance against whom? And what, concretely, did he think and do then?
Has he ever stopped to consider the responsibility he assumes when he encourages people to resist while being unable to protect them?
The positive counterpart of pity is protection. That applies even more strongly, more directly, and indeed absolutely to the right of resistance.
You grant someone a right that he is then supposed to obtain and fight for by himself.

In that case, please also leave it to him to decide whether, when, and how he will exercise it. These “legal thinkers” simply abstract away from the eternal connection between protection and obedience, persecution and resistance.
One can give the ambiguous term “rule-of-law state” a precise meaning by saying:
The rule-of-law state is a political community that replaces the right of resistance with a legal route of appeal through established institutions. What is involved is the elimination of resistance.
In concrete terms: feud and revolution.
In more modern language: sabotage, high treason, treason against the state, collaboration with the enemy. So begin by demanding the abolition of those criminal laws. That would be disarmament!
The rule-of-law state abolishes the idea of the internal enemy. That makes sense only if the actual enmity really comes to an end.
If this connection between the rule-of-law state and the ending of civil war is forgotten or concealed, then all the dangers of “pre-modern” life are summoned back into existence.
Few people today are capable of facing those dangers.
Most do not even want to be capable of facing them.
Under such circumstances one should not proclaim general theories about a resurrected right of resistance.
Typical of the Swiss and others who sit safely far from the firing line while laying down ethical and legal demands for everyone else.
Before God, everything that lies in the future has already happened.
What strikes us as the present is like a ray of light from a distant star that disappeared long ago: light still travelling onward even though its source has already gone out.
The justice of the divine order of the world therefore consists in its ignoring what we ourselves experience as our present.
When God allowed hundreds of thousands of Jews to be killed, he already saw at the same time the revenge they would take upon Germany.
And what he sees today in those who take revenge and exact retribution will be experienced by human beings in some unexpectedly different future present.
The mechanism by which day turns into night, light into darkness, solid into liquid, and so on becomes most abstract in the opposition between yesterday and tomorrow.
The past: fixed, unchangeable, completely closed.
The future: full, infinitely undetermined, even empty.
This mechanism is so stupidly mechanical that it must be wrong.
The future is not open and the past is not closed.
The past is not full and the future is not empty.
Law refers to the past, not the present, and binds us to the past.
Law is a worldly rule made by human beings for human beings—that is, a rule agreed upon in nominalist fashion. It is a rule fixed in advance, something already given.
All of that already belongs to the rule-of-law state:
anteceding law, the regula, the rule laid down beforehand. But that is only one possibility—the one I called “normativist.”

Decisionist law, by contrast, comes into being only at the moment of decision. And the law of every concrete order exists in a permanent present. So the binding force of the past applies only to the regula.
Is Luther’s binding of Christianity to Scripture—“The Word they still shall let remain!”—not itself a binding to the past?
Is it not narrower and more rigid than the regula fidei, the rule of faith, of Catholic dogma?
Does every act of turning something into dogma also turn it into law?
